legs.note: Straight lines between the stations whose positions do not depend on the route, sampled every 1 m.
legs.s2Rule: First leg, in walking order, whose straight line crosses ground steeper than 15 degrees.

route.method: A* over the 2 m terrain grid, 8 neighbours, by src/mission/route.js (run through tools/route_cli.mjs). A cell is walkable when its slope is at most 15 degrees; a diagonal step also needs both cells it passes between to be walkable. Cost = walking time (pace ASSUMPTIONS above). Lengths are horizontal map distances. The route runs START, S4, S5, START; S2 and S3 are points on its first leg (see their positionBasis).
route.maxSlopeNote: Steepest ground under the route: bilinear terrain slope sampled every 0.5 m along it.
route.stationCountRule: Stations walked to: every entry of order except START (S1, the briefing, is in the cabin).

direct.note: Straight line between the two stations against the planned route between the same two. Same pace rule for both; the straight line ignores the slope limit. Its time uses heights every 2 m, its slope samples are every 1 m.

route.endsNote: Route ends are the nearest terrain sample centre that can be reached on foot from the start; movedM is how far that is from the station.

traverse.source: data/layers/traverses.geojson (Perseverance, NASA/JPL MMGIS), clipped to the patch; one line per unbroken stretch inside the patch
traverse.solsFrom: data/stops/m20.json. The traverse file carries no sols (its only property is the rover name). Each drive line ends at a rover waypoint (matched within 0.5 m); a point's sol is the sol of the waypoint that ends its drive.
traverse.solRangeBasis: Lowest and highest sol among the drives that have any part inside the patch (a drive that crosses the patch edge counts). The same sols are on the points of the lines below.

computedNote: Values for the {placeholders} in card texts. The page recomputes the route-dependent ones (route_km, extra_min, station_count, direct_max_slope) from route.points and the terrain when it loads.

F1.text: Perseverance landed in Jezero crater on 18 Feb 2021 (Octavia E. Butler Landing site).

F2.text: The delta is a massive fan-shaped collection of rocks and sediment on the crater's western edge, built where a river met a crater lake billions of years ago; it rises about 40 m (130 ft) above the crater floor.

F3.text: Scientists think fine-grained sediment at the delta's base was once mud on the bottom of Lake Jezero; higher up are sand and rock fragments carried from upstream. JPL calls it one of the best places on Mars to look for signs of ancient microbial life.

F4.text: Crater-floor rocks are igneous: Séítah is coarsely crystalline, olivine-rich rock formed at the base of a magma body; Máaz is lava flows or the chemical counterpart. Water altered them. Cores are stored aboard Perseverance for potential return to Earth.

F5.text: At the delta front the team found sandstones, siltstones and boulder-rich conglomerates, interpreted as deposited underwater by density currents in a distal deltaic setting; boulder-rich conglomerates are consistent with high-energy floods.

F6.text: One sol = 24 h 39 min 35 s (NASA says about 24.6 h).

F7.text: EVA precedent: NASA's Artemis EVA concept of operations (EVA-EXP-0075, 2020): EVAs of up to 8 h, up to 2 km from the lander, terrain up to 20 degrees (Moon). Our 8 h EVA, 1 h reserve, 15 degree slope limit, 3.3 km/h pace and 20 min per stop are ASSUMPTIONS.
F7.source: NASA EVA-EXP-0075 (Artemis EVA concept of operations summary, Feb 2020)

F8.text: Astronauts can make connections, solve problems quickly and apply context in real time.

F9.text: Photo: MRO HiRISE, 25 cm per pixel. Terrain: USGS HiRISE stereo model, 1 m (shown at 2 m).
F9.source: MRO HiRISE; USGS HiRISE terrain model

S1.title: Briefing
S1.text: Today's Marswalk: Jezero crater delta. Perseverance landed here on 18 February 2021. The delta is a fan of rock and sediment built where a river met a crater lake billions of years ago. Plan: {route_km} km, {station_count} stops, back before the clock runs out.
S1.source: Sources: Team Protikriti data-sources.md; JPL news, 19 Apr 2022

S2.title: Read the ground
S2.text: Slope matters. We assume suited explorers avoid ground steeper than 15 degrees (ASSUMPTION; NASA's Artemis plan cites up to 20 degrees for the Moon). Turn on the slope layer: amber 10-15, red above 15. The straight line reaches {direct_max_slope} degrees; the planned route stays under 15 and takes {extra_min} more minutes.
S2.source: Sources: NASA EVA-EXP-0075 (Artemis EVA concept of operations summary, Feb 2020); MRO HiRISE; USGS HiRISE terrain model

S3.title: Follow the rover
S3.text: The orange line is Perseverance's real path. Inside this patch it drove between sols {sol_min} and {sol_max} (a sol is a Mars day, 24 h 39 min). Rovers scout; people can look, decide and adapt on the spot: astronauts solve problems quickly and apply context in real time.
S3.source: Sources: NASA/JPL MMGIS traverse; NASA GISS Mars24 / NASA Science; Space Apps challenge text

S4.title: Berea: first core
S4.text: Berea. Sample #19, Melyn, sealed on sol 749 (30 March 2023). NASA classes it a sedimentary rock core, 6.04 cm (2.38 in) long. NASA's list showed it aboard the rover (retrieved 2026-09-29). Position is approximate (rover waypoint, sol 736). Coring here is simulated.
S4.source: Source: NASA Science, Mars Rock Samples

S5A.title: Ridge lookout
S5A.text: Four cores were sealed here in 2022: Swift Run (sol 490, 6.69 cm), Skyland (495, 5.85 cm), Hazeltop (509, 5.97 cm), Bearwallow (516, 6.24 cm). NASA classes all four sedimentary. At the delta front the team found sandstones, siltstones and boulder-rich conglomerates laid down underwater.
S5A.source: Sources: NASA Science, Mars Rock Samples; Williams et al., LPSC 2023 abstract (NTRS 20230000588)
S5A.coreLocationsNote: Where each tube is now, from NASA's list (retrieved 2026-09-29)

S5B.title: Igneous vs sedimentary

columns.heading: Igneous (crater floor)
columns.text: Cooled from magma or lava. Séítah is olivine-rich; Máaz is lava flows or related. Near the landing area NASA classes {n_igneous} cores as igneous (sols {ig_min} to {ig_max}).

columns.heading: Sedimentary (delta)
columns.text: Laid down by water: sandstones, siltstones, conglomerates.

S5B.source: Sources: NASA Science, Mars Rock Samples (core counts); Farley et al. 2022, Science 377, eabo2196; Williams et al., LPSC 2023 abstract (NTRS 20230000588); JPL news, 19 Apr 2022
